Subject and Object Relative Clauses

When you want to clarify which person or thing you are talking about, you use a relative clause. Relative clauses modify a noun. You use a relative clause to add information to a sentence without beginning a new one.

You can begin a relative clause with who for people, which for things or that for either people or things.

In spoken English you usually use that, rather than which or who.
You put the relative clause immediately after the noun it talks about.
You can put the relative clause after the subject or the object of the sentence. We can't omit the relative pronoun (that, who, which).
A subject relative clause gives information about the subject of the clause and comes after the subject of the sentence.

For example:
The first tip that is listed is “Don't be a copycat candidate.”
Which tip? The tip that is listed. The clause that is listed immediately follows tip - the noun it describes.
An object relative clause describes the object of the clause and comes after the object of the sentence.

For example:
We can't underestimate peers who are a source of career opportunities.
Which peers? The peers who are a source of career opportunities.
A defining relative clause specifies which noun you are talking about:

• People who rely too much on searching on the Internet are missing opportunities.
  • (If you don't include 'who rely too much on searching on the internet', we don't know which people you are talking about).
A non-defining relative clause provides extra, non-essential information about something. This information is not necessary for us to understand the sentence.

• We can't underestimate peers, who are a source of career opportunities.
  • (We know peers are, so 'who are a source of career opportunities' is extra information).

Tag Questions with positive tags
You use tag questions to ask for clarification and confirmation.
A question tag is a short question that is added at the end of a statement.
They are mostly used in spoken English when you want to:

• confirm whether something is true or not true, or
  • to prompt a reply from the person we are speaking to.

A negative statement is followed by an affirmative question tag.
Use this when you think the other person will agree by saying ‘no'.
If the main verb is to be or a modal verb, the tag will be the same.
For all other main verbs, use the tag do/does or did/didn't. Look at the examples in the chart.

images.text:
Kristi: Hey Bianca! What are you doing here?
Bianca: I thought I'd come to give you a little moral support. Also, it can't hurt for me to see what types of jobs are out there, can it?
Kristi: Well, I'm glad you're here. Someone gave me a list of job search tips which I'm not sure I completely understand. I don't have to do all of them, do I?
Bianca: I don't know. Let's check them out.

Kristi: The first tip that is listed is “Don't be a copycat candidate.” That means to be different. I shouldn't do what everyone else does, should I?
Bianca: No. You want to stand out. It says “Take into consideration your personal experiences and career goals, which can be used to position yourself as a unique candidate.”
Kristi: It also says to make a good first impression, especially on social media. Employers who can see what we post on Twitter and Facebook might get a bad impression. We don't want them to see something embarrassing, do we?

Bianca: No way! I like this one: “Network with your peers.” People who rely too much on searching on the Internet are missing opportunities. All the jobs I've gotten have been because someone recommended me. It's so important to let all your peers know that you are looking for work, and what type of work you want.
Kristi: You're right. We can't underestimate peers who are a source of career opportunities. This is a great one too: “Be realistic: make sure you have both the skills and the commitment to be successful.”
Bianca: Wise advice. Okay, let's eat. You're not going to skip lunch, are you?
